summary: Describes HZ, a format for exchanging files with a mix of Chinese and ASCII characters. The content is identical to an article the author wrote in 1989. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: HZ is a 7-bit format for files that mix Chinese characters encoded in GB with ASCII text. Escape sequences mark when the text switches between ASCII and Chinese modes.

questions: how to mix chinese and ascii in one file
how does hz escape sequence work
how does hz switch between ascii and gb modes
what do the hz escape sequences mean
does hz impose a maximum line length
subtitle: A 7-bit format for text that mixes GB Chinese characters and ASCII.

tldr.problem: Text containing both Chinese and ASCII needed a 7-bit format for exchange through ASCII-based email systems.
tldr.mechanism: HZ uses ASCII mode by default and escape sequences to switch to two-byte GB character mode and back.
tldr.outcome: The memo describes a data format for mixed Chinese and ASCII text and rules for encoding and decoding it.

today: RFC 1843 is Informational and describes the HZ format for mixed Chinese and ASCII text. The memo does not specify an Internet standard.

sections.title: Why HZ Uses a 7-Bit Format
sections.content:
Many systems represented mixed Chinese and ASCII text using 8-bit codes, but exchanging such files through ASCII email systems required a 7-bit format. HZ encodes mixed GB and ASCII text in 7 bits and is also intended for terminal emulators that display and edit such files.

The memo assumes Chinese characters have already been encoded in GB2312-80. It does not cover the ROC BIG-5 standard.
sections.plainLanguage: HZ lets a file contain both GB-encoded Chinese and ASCII while using a 7-bit format. It assumes the Chinese characters have already been converted to GB.

sections.title: ASCII and GB Modes
sections.content:
HZ has two modes, with ASCII mode as the default. In ASCII mode, a tilde is an escape character: ~~ represents a literal tilde, ~{ switches to GB mode, and ~ marks a line continuation that produces no output.

In GB mode, data is read two bytes at a time as GB codes until ~} switches back to ASCII mode. The encoder surrounds a sequence of GB codes with ~{ and ~}.
sections.plainLanguage: The markers ~{ and ~} switch into and out of Chinese-character mode. The doubled tilde ~~ represents a tilde in the text.

sections.title: Line Length and Encoding Style
sections.content:
The format has no limit on line length, and a decoder does not need to process text according to lines. For compatibility with line- and page-oriented utilities, the RFC RECOMMENDS that encoders keep lines under 80 characters; this is an encoding style, not part of the HZ format.

The memo says an encoder or decoder needs to look ahead by at most one character. It also describes a line-continuation marker for splitting long lines without adding a newline to the decoded output.
sections.plainLanguage: HZ itself does not set a maximum line length. The RFC recommends shorter lines for some utilities, but calls that a style choice rather than a format rule.

references.text: Lee, Fung Fung, "HZ - A Data Format for Exchanging Files of Arbitrarily Mixed Chinese and ASCII Characters", September 4, 1989.
